original_question: For a fixed nonzero integer k, are there only finitely many integer solutions with p,q,x,y > 1 to the equation x^p - y^q = k?
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's formulation essentially verbatim: it fixes a nonzero integer k, asks for finiteness of the solution set, uses the equation x^p - y^q = k, and imposes p, q, x, y > 1 with all variables integral.
refined_question: Fix a nonzero integer k. Are there only finitely many quadruples (p, q, x, y) of integers with p, q, x, y > 1 such that x^p - y^q = k?
justification: The relevant target is exactly Unsolved Problem 20 in the paper. Its statement is the same finiteness question for the Diophantine equation x^p - y^q = k with fixed nonzero integer k and integer variables p, q, x, y all greater than 1. The immediately following parenthetical note identifies the special case k = 1 as Catalan's conjecture, confirming that your draft is aimed at this precise fixed-k finiteness problem and should not be broadened.
